quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: Correct, common Spanish is struck through as a mistake. Textbooks teach the indicative here, and that is a fair default, but negated dudar admits both moods: the indicative asserts, the subjunctive concedes. The course itself uses the subjunctive here: all 9 bank rows with *no dudo que* (u44-0915 to u44-1533) are subjunctive, and none is indicative, so the learner is told a form is wrong and later drilled on nothing else. Tested through the real card code: typing it fails with the hint "Check the verb ending: when does it happen?"
authority: Decisive: internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u44.json. Also Nueva gramatica ch. 25 and Butt and Benjamin ch. 16, from memory, not checkable online; native speaker reports on tomisimo and Lawless Spanish

quote: The flip side: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *No dudo que tienes razón*.
problem: Presents the indicative as the only option. A good rule keeps the plain verb as the default and says the other exists, which also follows from the course's own model: stating it as a fact versus granting it.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: The flip side: *No dudo que* says you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *No dudo que tienes razón*. You will also meet the wish form here, often before a *pero*: *No dudo que tengas razón, pero...* Both are correct.

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: States the indicative as obligatory. Same issue as the rule.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: *No dudo que* usually takes the indicative, because it is certainty, but the subjunctive is also correct.

quote: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *tienes*.
problem: The fill-in offers *tienes* or *tengas* with accept empty, so the correct *tengas* is marked wrong. Either accept both or remove the item.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: Set accept to ["No dudo que tengas razón."] and why to: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *tienes*.

quote: Llámame antes que salgas.
problem: Correct Spanish is struck through. *Antes que* and *antes de que* are both valid before a clause. The real slip English speakers make is dropping *que*.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes (equal examples: Llegara antes que anochezca, Llegara antes de que anochezca), read via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/antes
replacement: {"wrong":"Llámame antes de salgas.","right":"Llámame antes de que salgas.","why":"Almost. When a new person does the second action, you need *que*: *antes de que*."}

quote: *Antes de que* needs the *de*, then the wish form *salgas*.
problem: Claims the *de* is required. Accept should also include *Llámame antes que salgas.*
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes
replacement: *Antes de que* is followed by the wish form: *salgas*.

quote: Dijo que vendrá.
problem: *Dijo que vendrá* is correct whenever the coming is still ahead of the speaker now, and it is very common in Latin America. The rule that the future must shift is false as an absolute. The form is only wrong when the event lies in the past story.
authority: Nueva gramatica, ch. 24, double access, from memory; standard accounts agree the form needs the present perspective
replacement: {"wrong":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendrá, pero no vino.","right":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendría, pero no vino.","why":"Almost. She did not come, so the coming belongs to the past story: use the would form. *Dijo que vendrá* only works if it is still ahead of you now."}

quote: Teachers call this reported speech with backshift: the pluperfect stands in for the past and the conditional for the future, seen from a moment in the past.
problem: Contradicts u25 g:reported-past-basic, which says "Something already in the past stays put: *Joaquín se fue* → *Dijo que Joaquín se fue*." Here *Llamé* must become *había llamado*. Neither script says both are right. In Colombian speech the simple past is the more usual choice.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on tense concord (24); usage
replacement: Teachers call this reported speech with backshift: the pluperfect stands in for the past and the conditional for the future, seen from a moment in the past. In everyday Latin American speech the simple past often stays: *Dijo que llamó tres veces*. Both are right.

quote: Almost. A rate such as "three times a day" is always *por*.
problem: False. *Tres veces al día* and *una vez a la semana* are at least as common, and the bank itself has 45 such rows against 10 with *por* (u03-0538, u09-0013, u35-0090). A learner who trusts "always" will think the commonest form is wrong.
authority: Usage; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u03.json and u09.json
replacement: Almost. A rate never takes *para*. Say *por día* or, just as often, *al día*: *tres veces al día*.

quote: Spanish always keeps *que* and the changed ending.
problem: False for *recomendar*, *aconsejar* and *sugerir*, which also take an infinitive: *Te recomiendo hablar con un abogado*. The bank has it: u21-0749 *Te aconsejo hablar con un abogado*, u31-0864, u35-0049.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16); internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u21.json
replacement: Spanish uses *que* and the form you know from *quiero que*. With *recomendar*, *aconsejar* and *sugerir* you will also meet the infinitive: *Te recomiendo hablar con un abogado.* Both are right.

quote: Never add *pero* next to any of them. Each one already carries the "but".
problem: *Pero aun así* is normal Spanish. The bank has 9 rows, all in u38 and u39, the units that teach this (u38-0316, u38-0317, u38-0354, u39-0041, u39-0047, u39-0786), and this script's own PERSONAL prompt says *Estoy cansado, pero aun así…*. Only *pero sin embargo* is frowned on.
replacement: Don't add *pero* in front of *sin embargo*: it already carries the "but". *Pero aun así* is fine: *Estoy cansado, pero aun así voy.*

quote: Keep the *de*, and keep the *que* before a verb.
problem: *A pesar de* takes a plain infinitive with no *que*: *A pesar de estar cansada, Vale terminó los panes* (u39-0002, u38-0350). "Before a verb" will push learners to *a pesar de que estar*. The same claim is in pitfalls[1].why and yourTurn[4].why, and yourTurn[4] should accept *A pesar de estar cansado, Tomás trabaja.*
authority: Usage; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u38.json and u39.json
replacement: Keep the *de*, and keep the *que* before a conjugated verb. Before an infinitive there is no *que*: *A pesar de estar cansada, Vale terminó los panes.*

quote: Almost. Before a verb you need *que*: *a pesar de que* + verb.
problem: Same false generalisation as the rule.
replacement: Almost. Before a conjugated verb you need *que*: *a pesar de que llueve*. Before an infinitive, no *que*: *a pesar de estar cansado*.

quote: Spanish does not say 'the last one' for 'the latter'; *esta* does the pointing.
problem: False. *Este último* and *esta última* are the commonest way to say the latter, and the bank uses them in the same unit: u39-0724 *esta última es más barata*, u39-0727 *este último no quiso dar su nombre*. Delete this pitfall.
authority: Usage; Butt and Benjamin on demonstratives; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u39.json

quote: *Este*, *esta* point to the last thing you named: 'the latter'.
problem: Teaches bare *este* only. In modern prose *este último* is more frequent and less stiff, and bare *este* for a person can sound brusque in speech.
replacement: *Este*, *esta* point to the last thing you named: 'the latter'. *Este último* and *esta última* do the same job and are the safer choice.

quote: After a preposition you need an article or *quien*, not a bare *que*.
problem: False as a general rule. Bare *que* is standard after short prepositions with things and times: *el día en que llegó*, *la forma en que habla* (u34-1118, u46-1364). The example itself is correctly rejected, but only because the antecedent is a person.
replacement: With a person, a preposition needs an article or *quien*, not a bare *que*. With things and times a bare *que* is common after *en*: *el día en que llegó*.

quote: In Spanish it always comes first, in front of the thing you're describing: *los amigos con los que vivo*.
problem: Wrong description. In *los amigos con los que vivo* the preposition is after the noun being described. It goes in front of *los que*. Read literally this yields *con los amigos que vivo*.
replacement: In Spanish it always moves up, in front of *el que* or *quien*: *los amigos con los que vivo*.

quote: *Cada* always points at one at a time, so the noun stays singular.
problem: False with a number: *cada dos horas*, *cada ocho horas*. These are in the same unit (u33-0705, u33-0706, u33-0707) and in u35-0101 at the doctor.
replacement: *Cada* points at one at a time, so the noun stays singular. The exception is a number: *cada dos días*, *cada ocho horas*.

quote: Watch the *no*. *No se debe fumar* says you shouldn't. *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to.
problem: *No hay que* also expresses a prohibition or strong advice: *No hay que olvidar*. The course translates it as "we mustn't" 12 times at u56 (u56-0104, u56-0374). The contrast is a useful default, not a fact about the phrase.
replacement: Watch the *no*. *No se debe fumar* says you shouldn't. *No hay que pagar* usually says there's no need to, though with verbs like *olvidar* it means you mustn't: *No hay que olvidar*.

quote: You mustn't be afraid.
problem: A valid reading of *No hay que tener miedo* is offered as a wrong answer. Replace the distractor with one that is actually wrong.
replacement: You aren't afraid.

quote: Almost. Never use the *would* form after *si*; that spot always takes the *ra* form.
problem: True only of the conditional *si*. With *si* meaning whether, taught at u37, the would form is correct: u38-0416 *Me pregunto si Rosa estaría contenta con nosotros*. A learner who trusts "never" will reject this.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry si; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u38.json
replacement: Almost. In an *if* sentence, never use the *would* form after *si*; that spot takes the *ra* form. *Si* meaning *whether* is different: *No sé si vendría.*

quote: The *would* form never follows *si*; this spot takes the *ra* form.
problem: Same overreach. Limit the claim to *como si*.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry si
replacement: The *would* form never follows *como si*; this spot takes the *ra* form.

quote: Almost. After *lo* the adjective always stays in its basic masculine form.
problem: False at u47, where g:lo-que-intensity teaches agreement after *lo*: *lo cansada que estoy*. Limit the claim to this pattern.
replacement: Almost. In this pattern, the adjective after *lo* stays in its basic masculine form.

quote: *Nunca* goes before *había*; nothing can sit between *had* and the verb ending.
problem: Wrong diagnosis. In *Había visto nunca* the *nunca* is not between the two parts. The sentence fails because *nunca* after the verb needs *no*. The script itself accepts *Rosa no había viajado nunca sola*.
authority: Negative concord; internal contradiction within the script
replacement: Almost. *Nunca* goes before *había*. If it comes after the verb, Spanish also needs *no*: *No había visto nunca tanta gente.*

quote: Spanish marks that by switching the verb to the wish form: *tengas*, *esté*, *sea*, *venga*.
problem: The label "wish form" gives the wrong reason for the mood. Nobody wishes anything in *No creo que tengas razón*, *Dudo que venga*, *Es una pena que cierren* or *No conozco a nadie que sepa*. In *Me da miedo que venga* the event is the opposite of a wish. A learner who uses the label as a cue will choose the indicative after doubt, fear and dislike. The learner-visible label also fragments: across the 224 B1 scripts the same form is called wish form, wish ending, changed ending, asking form, other vowel, opposite ending, request ending, new verb form and -e style verb. Replace by one name and one concept everywhere (see report section 6).
authority: Nueva gramatica, chapter on mood (25): the indicative asserts, the subjunctive does not; pedagogical judgement

quote: *Te recomiendo* + *que* + a new verb form.
problem: At u32 the form is not new: the learner has used it since u21 and in every script from u28 to u30. It is presented as new, with its endings retaught, and renamed "asking form". Three days later it is "the other vowel", three days after that "the wish form".
authority: Internal: g:subj-wanting (u21), g:subj-opinion-negated (u28), g:subj-cuando-future (u32 d4), g:subj-purpose-full (u32 d7)
replacement: *Te recomiendo* + *que* + the form you already know from *quiero que*.

quote: The verb after *que* is for the other person's action, and it changes its ending to the "asking" form.
problem: Same issue: a new name for a known form.
replacement: The verb after *que* is for the other person's action, and it takes the same form you use after *quiero que*.

quote: *Decir que* or *pedir que*, then a verb with the "opposite" ending:
problem: At u37 the form has had a dozen outings under other names. "Opposite" and "request ending" are further labels for it.
replacement: *Decir que* or *pedir que*, then the form you already know from *quiero que*:

quote: Teachers call this the subjunctive: the mood Spanish uses when one person wants another to do something.
problem: Defines the whole mood by one of its uses. The learner has by now used it for doubt, emotion, time and relative clauses, none of which fits this definition.
replacement: Teachers call this the subjunctive after a verb of request. It is the same form you use after *quiero que*, *dudo que* and *cuando*.

quote: If you mean people in general, skip *que* and use the plain verb: *Es normal tener miedo.* *Es mejor llamar antes.*
problem: Three days earlier (u28 d1) "plain verb" was defined as the indicative: *tienes*, *está*, *es*. Here it means the infinitive. Following the earlier definition gives *Es normal tiene miedo*. Of 23 B1 scripts that say plain verb or plain form, some mean indicative and some infinitive.
authority: Internal: g:subj-opinion-negated smallPrint "The plain form is the indicative."
replacement: If you mean people in general, skip *que* and use the infinitive: *Es normal tener miedo.* *Es mejor llamar antes.*

quote: It's about people in general, so no *que*: just the plain verb.
problem: Same collision.
replacement: It's about people in general, so no *que*: just the infinitive.

quote: When it is about people in general, use the plain verb and no *que*.
problem: Same collision.
replacement: When it is about people in general, use the infinitive and no *que*.

quote: When the same person does both things, drop *que* and use the plain verb: *Abro temprano para encontrar todo listo.* *Llámame antes de salir.*
problem: Same collision: here plain verb means infinitive.
replacement: When the same person does both things, drop *que* and use the infinitive: *Abro temprano para encontrar todo listo.* *Llámame antes de salir.*

quote: When the same person does both things, *que* disappears and the verb stays plain.
problem: Same collision.
replacement: When the same person does both things, *que* disappears and you use the infinitive.

quote: Almost. If you do both things yourself, skip *que* and use the plain verb.
problem: Same collision.
replacement: Almost. If you do both things yourself, skip *que* and use the infinitive.

quote: The second action belongs to someone else, so its verb takes the wish form: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.
problem: Gives the wrong cause. A change of subject explains *que* versus the infinitive. It does not explain the mood: *Llamo porque vienes* has a change of subject and takes the indicative. The mood comes from the second action being not yet real.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: The second action belongs to someone else, so you need *que*. It hasn't happened yet when you plan it, so its verb takes the form you know from *quiero que*: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.

quote: The verb after *que* tells your listener whether the thing is real or only wished for.
problem: *No conozco a nadie que sepa* is not wished for. The test the script itself uses is better.
replacement: The verb after *que* tells your listener whether you know the thing exists.

quote: two take the wish form, one never does.
problem: Contradicts the rule, which says *quizás* and *tal vez* take either form.
replacement: two can take the wish form, one never does.

quote: Busco un apartamento que tiene dos cuartos.
problem: Struck through as wrong, but this script's readAndPick[2] teaches the same shape as correct: *Busco a una abogada que sabe de arriendos* means a particular lawyer. x:relative-ind-subj also says the article does not decide. Indefinite plus indicative is correct when you have one in mind.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: {"wrong":"Busco un apartamento que tiene dos cuartos.","right":"Busco un apartamento que tenga dos cuartos.","why":"Almost. If you haven't found it and any one will do, use the wish ending: *tenga*. *Que tiene* would mean you already have one in mind."}

quote: Almost. *El apartamento* is one you already know about, so the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.
problem: Ties the mood to the article. That contradicts x:relative-ind-subj ("The article helps... but it doesn't decide") and will collide with *el que quiera* at u50 (g:subj-free-relatives).
authority: Internal; Nueva gramatica on relatives and mood
replacement: Almost. If you mean one particular apartment you know, the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.

quote: Busco a una abogada que sepa de arriendos.
problem: Personal *a* signals a specific person, which pulls against the subjunctive reading this item teaches ("any lawyer, if there is one"). The bank mostly gets this right: 7 rows drop the *a* (u33-0039, u33-0054, u33-0055) against 2 that keep it (u33-0523, u33-0960). Dropping it also shows a second cue for the same idea.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16), personal a
replacement: Busco una abogada que sepa de arriendos.

quote: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape.
problem: The node title and example promise *siento que*, but the script never uses it and no script teaches the meaning switch. *Siento que estés triste* is I'm sorry you're sad; *Siento que estás triste* is I sense you're sad. Both moods are in the bank (u30-0037, u30-1135, u25-0392), and p:sentir-lo-de strikes the indicative through as wrong. This is the sharpest mood contrast in the emotion family and English speakers will not guess it.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape. One trap: *siento que* with the wish form means I'm sorry: *Siento que estés triste.* With the plain verb it means I feel or I sense: *Siento que estás triste.*

quote: Feelings about someone else call for the *tengas* form, not *tienes*.
problem: *Siento que tienes que irte* is correct Spanish with a different meaning. Keep the pitfall but say why.
replacement: To say you are sorry about it, use the *tengas* form. *Siento que tienes que irte* means *I feel you have to leave*.

quote: *Puede que* + wish form
problem: The bank drills 18 rows with *no es cierto que* or *no es verdad que* and 14 with *es imposible que* in u29, for example u29-0600 and u29-0624, tagged g:subj-doubt. No script in the course names either frame. x:fact-value teaches that *es verdad que* takes the plain verb and never says that denying it flips the mood.
authority: Internal; Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement:
*Puede que* + wish form

The same goes when you deny a fact or rule it out: *No es cierto que el café pierda plata.* *Es imposible que lo sepa.*

quote: The same goes for *en cuanto* (as soon as) and *hasta que* (until).
problem: The bank drills *después de que* (u32-0103 to u32-0107) and *tan pronto como* (u32-0100) under this node, but the script names neither, and no script in the course teaches *después de que*. *Apenas*, the everyday Colombian as soon as, is also missing.
replacement: The same goes for *en cuanto* and *apenas* (as soon as), *después de que* (after) and *hasta que* (until).

quote: *irse* is leaving, and the place no longer matters: *Me voy*.
problem: *Irse* takes a destination all the time: *Me voy a la playa* (u22-0109), *se fue a Santa Marta* (u25-0274). The contrast x:ir-irse says it better: it looks back at where you are leaving.
replacement: *irse* is leaving. It looks back at where you are leaving from, so you can say just *Me voy*, or add where you're off to: *Me voy a Medellín*.

quote: When "se" changes the meaning: ir and irse, dormir and dormirse, quedar and quedarse
problem: The title promises *quedar* and *quedarse*, but the script gives only *quedarse*. The contrast is never shown. It replaces it with *parecer* and *parecerse*, and the closing question ("just doing it, or leaving, or starting it?") does not fit *parecerse*.
replacement: When "se" changes the meaning: ir and irse, dormir and dormirse, parecer and parecerse

quote: *Ponerse* + a word for a mood or colour: it hits you, then passes. *Me puse rojo. Se puso contento.*
problem: *Ponerse* also marks lasting visible changes, and the bank tags these to this node: u30-0550 *Mi tío se puso muy gordo*, u30-0582 *La situación se puso fea*. The learner is taught that the change passes and then drilled on one that does not.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16), verbs of becoming; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u30.json
replacement: *Ponerse* + a word for a mood, colour or look: a visible change, usually quick. *Me puse rojo. Se puso contento.*

quote: Fame is a status you reach over time, so *hacerse*; *ponerse* is only for quick moods and colours.
problem: Same as above, and it excludes *volverse famoso*, which is in the node title and in the bank (u30-0589, u30-0596).
replacement: Fame is a status you reach over time, so *hacerse* or *volverse*; *ponerse* is for a change in how someone looks or feels.

quote: Becoming something through effort uses *hacerse*.
problem: *Vale quiere volverse famosa* is natural, is what the node title says, and is marked wrong because accept lists only *Vale se quiere hacer famosa*.
replacement: Add to accept: "Vale quiere volverse famosa."

quote: English says *for arriving*, and so does Spanish: no *porque*, no changing the verb.
problem: Spanish does not say *for arriving*, it says *por llegar*. pitfalls[1] says the opposite: "Unlike English *for arriving*, Spanish uses the infinitive."
replacement: English says *for arriving*; Spanish says *por llegar*: no *porque*, and no *-ando* form.

quote: English uses different words for each job. Spanish keeps one verb and changes the ending.
problem: Untrue on both sides, in this script's own translations: *Debes descansar* is You must rest and *Debe de estar cansada* is She must be tired, so English uses *must* for both, and *debe* versus *debe de* differ by a word, not an ending.
replacement: English uses *must* for two of these jobs and *should* for the third. Spanish keeps one verb: the ending, or the little *de*, tells you which job it is doing.

quote: In fast speech people often drop the *de* from a guess, so listen to the meaning.
problem: Not a fast speech effect. Educated written usage also allows *deber* without *de* for probability.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry deber: deber + infinitive for probability is extended in cultivated usage (via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/deber)
replacement: People often drop the *de* from a guess, even in careful writing, so go by the meaning.

quote: In Latin America it often covers a recent finished action too, where English says simply *you came*.
problem: Not regional. Spanish has no present subjunctive for a finished past, so *hayas venido* corresponds to both *viniste* and *has venido* everywhere.
authority: Nueva gramatica, chapter on tense concord (24)
replacement: Spanish uses it for any finished action, even where English says simply *you came*.

quote: Mientras más temprano llegas, mejor.
problem: Addressed to a friend about an arrival still to come, this needs the subjunctive, by the rule learned at u32 ("is it still in the future?"). The indicative reads as a general truth about arrivals. Translation yourTurn[4] should make *llegues* the answer and keep *llegas* in accept.
authority: Internal: g:subj-cuando-future; Nueva gramatica on proportional comparatives
replacement: Mientras más temprano llegues, mejor.

quote: Comparing in numbers and degrees: el doble, más de la mitad, cada vez más, cuanto más…
problem: The title and the node sentence (*Ganamos el doble que el año pasado*) promise *el doble* and *más de la mitad*. The rule, examples and exercises teach neither. *El doble* has 0 rows in B1. *Mientras más* has 0 rows in u36 to u41 and 1 in the whole bank. Of 121 rows tagged to this node, 67 are plain *más de* or *menos de*.

quote: Fueron vendidos todos los almuerzos.
problem: Grammatical Spanish, struck through under "Almost everyone slips here", and g:passive-ser teaches this exact construction two units later. It is a register note, not an error. Delete it or move it to the rule.

quote: Joaquín asked Eulalia to make sure the family made peace.
problem: Adds "to make sure". The Spanish is *Joaquín le pidió a Eulalia que la familia hiciera las paces.*
authority: Translation rule set by the owner
replacement: Joaquín asked Eulalia for the family to make peace.

quote: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*.
problem: When the order is still pending, Latin American speakers commonly keep the present subjunctive: *Me dijo que la llame mañana*. This is accepted usage and the learner will meet it in Bogotá.
authority: Nueva gramatica, chapter on tense concord (24)
replacement: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*. If the order still stands, you will also hear the present: *Me dijo que la llame mañana.*

quote: You need *ojalá*, the Spanish way to say "I wish" and "if only".
problem: Presents *ojalá* as new at u41. The learner met it at u22 and spent u40 d1 (g:imperfect-subj) on this exact content, with the same sentences: *Ojalá pudiéramos quedarnos*, *Ojalá tuviera*, *Ojalá fuera*. Use this day for what u40 did not cover, such as *ojalá* with a person other than I, or merge the nodes.

quote: *Igual* at the start also means *maybe*, in casual talk.
problem: Wrong dialect, presented as Bogotá speech. The DPD marks *igual* for *maybe* as colloquial Spain. In American Spanish a sentence-initial *igual* is documented as concessive, *anyway*, *regardless*: *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. So the 21 bank rows likely mean something else in the setting they are written for: *Igual hace frío en la noche, lleva chaqueta* would read as It's cold at night anyway, not It might be cold. *De pronto* for maybe is correct Colombian usage and should stay. The rest of the rule, the examples, pitfalls[1] and the bank rows need rewriting with it.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry igual: used in the colloquial language of Spain with indicative for a lo mejor, posiblemente (via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/igual). American concessive igual: Garcia Negroni and Marcovecchio 2013, Llopis Cardona. No source found specific to Colombia, so a Colombian speaker should confirm the replacement wording
replacement: *Igual* at the start of a sentence usually means something else in Latin America: *anyway*. *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. In Spain it can mean maybe, so don't be surprised if a Spanish friend uses it that way.

quote: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time, and neither means what the dictionary says. In everyday speech, both mean *maybe*.
problem: Same issue.
replacement: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time. *De pronto* means *maybe*. *Igual* usually means *anyway*.

quote: Teachers call this a hope or expectation phrase. Like other wishes, it takes the subjunctive.
problem: *Confiar en que* also takes the future indicative, which may be the more usual choice: *Confío en que todo saldrá bien*. A learner who says this will be marked wrong and told it is not allowed.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: Teachers call this a hope or expectation phrase. It usually takes the subjunctive, but you will also meet the future: *Confío en que todo saldrá bien.*

quote: Spanish has no *ser* for size or weight. It uses a verb for each question:
problem: *Ser de* is common with measurements: *La mesa es de dos metros*, *El apartamento es de 70 metros*. What is wrong is *es dos metros* with no *de*.
replacement: Spanish doesn't say *es dos metros*. It uses a verb for each question:

quote: Sí, con gusto.
problem: Struck through as wrong, but *Sí, con gusto* or *Sí, claro* is a normal answer to *¿Te importaría...?* in real speech: the pragmatics of the request win over the literal logic. Keep the advice that *no* is the safe answer, not the claim that *sí* is a mistake.

quote: ¿Qué te ha parecido el restaurante?
problem: Struck through as wrong. It is correct Spanish, and the owner's policy is that Peninsular forms are accepted. The why is fine; the strikethrough is not. Reframe as a preference.
authority: Owner decision: Peninsular forms accepted as answers

quote: First, the plan: *pensaba* or *iba a*, in the imperfect, plus a plain verb.
problem: Plain verb means the infinitive here and the indicative elsewhere.
replacement: First, the plan: *pensaba* or *iba a*, in the imperfect, plus an infinitive.

quote: then *importaría*, then the plain verb: *¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?*
problem: Same collision.
replacement: then *importaría*, then the infinitive: *¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?*

quote: *Por* + a plain verb ending in *-r*: the reason is an action.
problem: Same collision. The -r gloss saves it, but the term should be one thing.
replacement: *Por* + an infinitive, the form ending in *-r*: the reason is an action.

quote: *A lo mejor* has no choice: plain verb, every time. *A lo mejor tengas razón* is a classic mistake.
problem: Fine as production advice, but false as a statement about Spanish, and this course is Latin American by decision. The DPD says *a lo mejor* takes the indicative almost always, while the subjunctive is also possible, especially in American Spanish. Keep the plain verb as the answer, drop "classic mistake".
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry mejor (via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/mejor)
replacement: *A lo mejor* takes the plain verb almost every time. You may hear the wish form in Latin America, but the plain verb is always right.

quote: Almost. Same rule: with *a lo mejor* the plain verb is the only choice.
problem: Same issue.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry mejor
replacement: Almost. Same rule: with *a lo mejor*, use the plain verb.

quote: Almost. The *de* belongs only to guesses, never to advice.
problem: The advice is right but "never" is too strong. The current DPD notes that *deber de* for obligation also occurs in cultivated usage, though much less often.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry deber (via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/deber; page itself not readable)
replacement: Almost. For advice, leave out the *de*. It belongs to guesses.

quote: He found the box before he opened it, so the earlier event takes *había*.
problem: *Abrió la caja que encontró* is grammatical, and Latin American speakers often leave order to the context. *Había encontrado* is clearer, not obligatory.
replacement: He found the box before he opened it. *Había encontrado* makes that order clear.

quote: Almost. English repeats "more and more", but Spanish uses *cada vez más*.
problem: *Más y más* is grammatical. It is less idiomatic, not wrong.
replacement: Almost. *Más y más* exists, but the everyday Spanish is *cada vez más*.

quote: *Pensar* here is not about opinions: for those, *pienso que* comes later.
problem: At u32 it does not come later. The bank has *pienso que* in 7 rows before u32, and the learner has used *creo que* since A2.
replacement: *Pensar* here is not about opinions: for those, use *pienso que*.

quote: Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; este trajo pan y aquella trajo jugo.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* is the nearer item and must agree with *mi prima*, so it should be *esta*; *aquel* points to the earlier *mi hermano*. As written, gender forces *este* onto the brother and *aquella* onto the cousin, which reverses the rule and contradicts the English ("the latter brought bread").
authority: g:referring-back rule; Nueva gramatica on demonstratives
replacement: Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; esta trajo pan y aquel trajo jugo.

quote: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Este habla y esta escucha.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* can only be Simón, the first named, so *este* is pointing at the former, and the English says "the latter talks". Two proximal demonstratives in a row also defeat the contrast. To match the English: Vale (latter) talks, Simón (former) listens.
replacement: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Esta habla y aquel escucha.

quote: Vale tiene una hermana y un hermano. Esta vive en Cali y aquel vive en Bogotá.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. The last named is *un hermano*, so the latter must be *este*. *Esta* can only be the sister, the first named. Spanish and English disagree on who lives where.
replacement: Vale tiene una hermana y un hermano. Este vive en Cali y aquella vive en Bogotá.

quote: Hernando conoció a Rosa en un taxi. Dicha noche cambió su vida.
problem: *Dicha noche* has no antecedent: no night was mentioned. The script says *dicho* means "the one I just mentioned". The English "That night in question" hides this.
replacement: {"es":"Hernando conoció a Rosa una noche en un taxi. Dicha noche cambió su vida.","en":"Hernando met Rosa one night in a taxi. That night changed his life."}

quote: Con Hernando; este me dio la lección.
problem: With only Hernando in the reply there is no pair, so *este* as "the latter" is out of place, and bare *este* for a person in speech sounds brusque.
authority: Usage; the script itself says these are for writing
replacement: {"es":"Con Hernando; él me dio la lección.","en":"With Hernando; he gave me the lesson."}

quote: Both books are by the same family, but the latter is older.
problem: No two books are named in order, so *este* cannot be "the latter". It means this one.
replacement: Both books are from the same family, but this one is older.

quote: Entonces lo anterior cambia el plan.
problem: *Lo anterior* is formal written Spanish, wrong in a spoken reply.
replacement: {"es":"Entonces eso cambia el plan.","en":"Then that changes the plan."}

quote: Vale no tiene tiempo hoy, y lo anterior es un problema para el plazo.
problem: A chatty clause with a report-writing phrase inside it. *Eso* is what anyone would say.
replacement: {"es":"Vale no tiene tiempo hoy, y eso es un problema para el plazo.","en":"Vale has no time today, and that is a problem for the deadline."}

quote: Simón tendría hambre por eso gritaba.
problem: Run-on: two clauses need a comma.
replacement: Simón tendría hambre, por eso gritaba.

quote: ¿Dónde estarías tú a las cinco ayer?
problem: Asks someone to guess where they themselves were. The English is equally odd.
replacement: {"es":"¿Dónde estaría Vale a las cinco ayer?","en":"Where do you think Vale was at five yesterday?"}

quote: Tomás se queda en Altamira hasta el viernes.
problem: Altamira is a hotel company and a man in the story, not a place.
authority: Story bible, chapters ch083 and ch099
replacement: {"es":"Tomás se queda en Taganga hasta el viernes.","en":"Tomás is staying in Taganga until Friday."}

quote: For me, the café in Altamira is the best.
problem: Altamira is a company, not a town.
replacement: For me, Altamira's coffee is the best.

quote: For me, the proposal is obviously good.
problem: *Muy* is dropped. The owner's rule is an exact translation.
replacement: For me, the proposal is obviously very good.

quote: Who does the lady say is calling?
problem: *¿De parte de quién pregunta la señora?* means on whose behalf she is asking. Nothing says she is calling.
replacement: Who is the lady asking on behalf of?

quote: Se me rompió el celular, pero me lavé las manos.
problem: The two halves have no connection, and *pero* implies one.
replacement: {"es":"Se me rompió el celular y me corté la mano.","en":"My phone broke and I cut my hand."}

quote: Es raro oír a Simón sin hablar.
problem: *Sin hablar* attaches to the hearer, not to Simón, and you cannot hear someone not talking.
replacement: {"es":"Es raro no oír a Simón.","en":"It's unusual not to hear Simón."}

quote: Antes de operar no se debe comer nada.
problem: *Operar* is what the surgeon does. The patient is meant here.
replacement: Antes de una operación no se debe comer nada.

quote: Si tuviera mejor humor, me reiría de todo esto.
problem: *Mejor humor* reads as a better mood. The English says a better sense of humour.
replacement: Si tuviera mejor sentido del humor, me reiría de todo esto.

quote: Un vecino nos guió hasta la alcaldía.
problem: Since the 2010 Ortografia, *guio* counts as one syllable and takes no accent. The story already spells *se rio* correctly in ch107. Check that the answer matcher still accepts the old spelling.
replacement: Un vecino nos guio hasta la alcaldía.

replacement: Rosa crio a su familia casi sola.

quote: Mi tío crió a tres nenes en un apartamento pequeño.

quote: Dado que mi tía no tuvo hijos, crió a su sobrino con mucho cariño.
problem: Since the 2010 Ortografia, *crio* counts as one syllable and takes no accent. The story already spells *se rio* correctly in ch107. Check that the answer matcher still accepts the old spelling.

quote: Insecurity is the biggest problem in the neighbourhood.
problem: In Colombian and general Latin American usage *inseguridad* is street crime, the lack of public safety. In English "insecurity" means self-doubt, so the card teaches a false friend.
authority: Usage; Diccionario de la lengua espanola, inseguridad
replacement: Crime is the biggest problem in the neighbourhood.

quote: Igual vendo el carro.
problem: 21 rows train *igual* as maybe, with English "might". In Colombia these read as *anyway*: *Igual vendo el carro* is I'm selling the car anyway. See claim on p:de-pronto-igual rule. Each row needs retranslating as anyway, or rewriting with *de pronto*.

quote: Llegamos a un compromiso: esperar una semana.
problem: The lexeme is glossed "commitment" but all six rows use it as "compromise", the false friend. *Llegar a un compromiso* exists in formal and political Spanish, so these are not ungrammatical, but the everyday word for a compromise is *un acuerdo* or *un arreglo*, and the main Colombian sense is missing: *Tengo un compromiso* (I have a prior engagement). Rewrite the rows around commitment and engagement, and teach the false friend explicitly.
authority: Diccionario de la lengua espanola, compromiso; Colombian usage

quote: profundar
problem: A dictionary word (DLE: profundar, tr., profundizar) but a poor B1 target. Its forms *profundo* and *profunda* are identical to the adjective, so its freqRank of 1926 is very likely inflated by adjective tokens. The lexeme comes from the freq source alone. Six rows, u40-0639 to u40-0644, drill it where everyday Spanish says *hacer más hondo*, *cavar más hondo* or *profundizar*. Delete the lexeme and rework the rows. A sweep of the freq source for verbs whose forms collide with adjectives is worthwhile.
authority: DLE entry profundar (via search snippet of dle.rae.es/profundar); frequency inference is mine, no corpus access

authority: Diccionario de la lengua espanola; seen in render.ts at unit 32
